posts.title: Optimizing PageSpeed, LCP & Core Web Vitals
posts.summary:
Website performance is more than just achieving a high score in Google PageSpeed Insights. A fast website improves user experience, reduces waiting time, and helps visitors interact with your website more smoothly.

Performance can also influence the overall page experience and SEO. The goal is not simply to achieve a perfect score, but to build a website that loads quickly, responds quickly, and remains visually stable.
posts.content:
Performance can also contribute to a good overall page experience. Google uses Core Web Vitals as part of its ranking systems, but a good PageSpeed score or good Core Web Vitals do not guarantee higher rankings. Relevant, helpful content and other search signals still matter.

The goal should not be to chase a perfect score. The goal is to build a website that loads quickly, responds quickly, remains visually stable, and provides a good experience for real users.

Check your website with Google PageSpeed Insights →

What Are Core Web Vitals?

Core Web Vitals are a set of user-focused metrics that measure important aspects of a webpage experience: loading performance, interactivity, and visual stability.

The current Core Web Vitals are LCP, INP, and CLS.

LCP — Largest Contentful Paint

LCP measures loading performance by measuring when the largest content element visible within the viewport is rendered.

For a good user experience, aim for an LCP of 2.5 seconds or less.

INP — Interaction to Next Paint

INP measures how responsive a page is to user interactions. It helps identify experiences where clicks, taps, or keyboard interactions take too long to produce a visual response.

A good INP is 200 milliseconds or less.

CLS — Cumulative Layout Shift

CLS measures visual stability. It tracks unexpected movement of visible content while a page is loading or changing.

A good CLS score is 0.1 or less.

How Are Core Web Vitals Evaluated?

Core Web Vitals are primarily real-user, or field, metrics. Google generally evaluates them at the 75th percentile of page visits, segmented across mobile and desktop.

This means that optimizing only your own development machine is not enough. A website should perform well across different devices, browsers, network conditions, and real-world users.

Learn more about Core Web Vitals and Google Search →

Why Does Website Performance Matter?

Website performance affects much more than a PageSpeed score. A faster and more stable website can provide:

  • Better user experience
  • Faster access to important content
  • Better mobile usability
  • More responsive interactions
  • Fewer visual disruptions
  • Better conversion opportunities
  • A stronger overall page experience

Performance also matters for SEO and search visibility, but it is important to understand the relationship correctly.

A perfect PageSpeed score does not automatically mean better Google rankings.

Google considers many signals, including the relevance and usefulness of content. Core Web Vitals are part of Google's page experience and ranking systems, but they are not a replacement for good content, technical SEO, accessibility, and a well-built website.

PageSpeed Insights: What Does It Actually Measure?

Google PageSpeed Insights provides both lab data and real-world field data.

  • Lab data: Generated using Lighthouse in a controlled, simulated environment. It is useful for debugging and finding performance opportunities during development.
  • Field data: Based on real-user experiences collected through the Chrome User Experience Report (CrUX), when data is available.

This is why your PageSpeed report and the experience of a real visitor may not always show exactly the same numbers.

PageSpeed Insights also provides audits and recommendations across areas such as Performance, Accessibility, Best Practices, and SEO.

How I Approach Website Performance Optimization

1. Optimize Images for Performance

Images are often among the largest resources downloaded by a webpage. Oversized or incorrectly optimized images can increase page weight, delay loading, and affect LCP.

Image optimization is therefore one of the first areas I investigate when improving website performance.

Use Modern Image Formats

Modern formats such as WebP and AVIF can often provide smaller files while maintaining good visual quality.

The important principle is to deliver an appropriately sized, high-quality image without sending unnecessary bytes to the browser.

Use the <picture> Element When Appropriate

The <picture> element is useful when you need to provide different image formats or different image sources depending on browser capabilities, screen characteristics, or art direction.

<picture>
    <source
        srcset="/images/hero.avif"
        type="image/avif"
    >

    <source
        srcset="/images/hero.webp"
        type="image/webp"
    >

    <img
        src="/images/hero.jpg"
        width="1200"
        height="700"
        alt="Website performance dashboard"
    >
</picture>

The browser can choose a supported source, while the <img> element provides the fallback.

The <picture> element is especially useful when you need different crops or compositions for different screen sizes.

Use srcset and sizes for Responsive Images

You do not always need <picture>. When you have different sizes of the same image, srcset and sizes on an <img> element are often the appropriate solution.

<img
    src="/images/product-800.webp"
    srcset="
        /images/product-400.webp 400w,
        /images/product-800.webp 800w,
        /images/product-1200.webp 1200w
    "
    sizes="
        (max-width: 600px) 100vw,
        (max-width: 1200px) 50vw,
        600px
    "
    width="1200"
    height="800"
    alt="Product image"
>

This allows the browser to choose an appropriate image resource based on the device and available display size rather than downloading the largest image for every visitor.

Always Provide Image Dimensions

When the dimensions are known, provide width and height attributes.

<img
    src="/images/product.webp"
    width="800"
    height="600"
    alt="Product image"
>

Providing dimensions allows the browser to reserve space for the image before it finishes loading. This helps reduce unexpected layout movement and can improve CLS.

Lazy Load Below-the-Fold Images

Images that are outside the initial viewport can often be lazy loaded. This allows the browser to prioritize resources required for the initial page view.

<img
    src="/images/gallery.webp"
    width="800"
    height="600"
    loading="lazy"
    alt="Gallery image"
>

However, lazy loading should not be applied blindly to every image.

Avoid lazy-loading important above-the-fold images, especially an image that is likely to be the LCP element.

Prioritize the LCP Image Carefully

If the main hero image is the LCP element, make sure the browser can discover it early and give it appropriate priority.

<img
    src="/images/hero.webp"
    width="1200"
    height="700"
    fetchpriority="high"
    alt="Website performance dashboard"
>

fetchpriority="high" can provide the browser with a hint that an important image should receive higher priority.

This should be used selectively. Marking too many resources as high priority can reduce the benefit of prioritization.

Use Meaningful Alt Text

The alt attribute provides alternative text for users who cannot see an image and also helps search engines understand the image.

<img
    src="/images/doctor-dashboard.webp"
    width="1200"
    height="700"
    alt="Doctor appointment dashboard showing today's patient queue"
>

Write alt text that describes the actual image or its purpose in context. Do not use the alt attribute as a place to stuff keywords.

Use HTML Images for Important Content

If an image is meaningful content, use an HTML <img> element instead of relying only on a CSS background image.

Prefer:

<img
    src="/images/team.webp"
    width="1200"
    height="700"
    alt="Development team working together"
>

Google can discover images from the src attribute of standard HTML image elements, including images inside <picture>. Google does not index CSS images in the same way.

Use Descriptive Image Filenames

Image filenames can provide additional context about the subject of an image.

Prefer:

doctor-appointment-dashboard.webp

Instead of:

IMG00023.webp

Keep filenames short, descriptive, and relevant to the actual image.

Compress and Resize Images Before Uploading

Do not upload a 4000px-wide image when the website only needs to display it at 800px. Resize the source appropriately and compress it before serving it.

  • Resize oversized images
  • Compress image files
  • Use WebP or AVIF where appropriate
  • Generate multiple image sizes when necessary
  • Use srcset and sizes for responsive images
  • Use <picture> when different sources are needed
  • Lazy-load appropriate below-the-fold images
  • Do not lazy-load the main LCP image
  • Provide image dimensions
  • Use meaningful alt text
  • Use descriptive filenames

Read the web.dev Image Performance Guide →

2. Optimize CSS

CSS is generally a render-blocking resource. The browser needs to download and process the required CSS before it can render the page.

Large or unnecessary stylesheets can therefore delay the initial rendering of a page.

  • Remove genuinely unused CSS
  • Minify production CSS
  • Split large stylesheets when appropriate
  • Keep critical styles lean
  • Avoid shipping large framework styles that are not needed
  • Load stylesheets as early as possible
  • Use media queries appropriately for conditional CSS

For example:

<link
    rel="stylesheet"
    href="/css/app.min.css"
>

Avoid loading a large CSS bundle on every page when a significant portion of it is never used. Chrome DevTools Coverage can help identify CSS that is not being used on a particular page.

Critical CSS

For some websites, critical CSS can be used to deliver the styles required for the initial viewport quickly while loading the remaining styles separately.

This is an advanced optimization and should be measured carefully. Inlining too much CSS can increase the size of the initial HTML and reduce caching benefits.

3. Optimize JavaScript

JavaScript can consume main-thread time and delay user interactions. Large scripts, long-running tasks, unnecessary libraries, and third-party scripts can all affect responsiveness and INP.

For scripts that are not required to execute before the document is parsed, defer can be useful:

<script
    src="/js/app.js"
    defer
></script>
  • Remove unused JavaScript
  • Minify production bundles
  • Code-split large applications
  • Defer non-critical scripts
  • Reduce unnecessary third-party scripts
  • Break up long-running JavaScript tasks
  • Avoid unnecessary DOM operations

JavaScript optimization is especially important for INP, because excessive main-thread work can make interactions feel slow.

4. Optimize Fonts

Fonts can add network requests and increase the amount of data that needs to be downloaded before text is displayed correctly.

Use only the font families and weights that your design actually needs. When self-hosting fonts, WOFF2 is a modern and widely supported format.

@font-face {
    font-family: "MyFont";
    src: url("/fonts/my-font.woff2") format("woff2");
    font-display: swap;
}
  • Use WOFF2 where appropriate
  • Reduce unnecessary font families
  • Reduce unnecessary font weights
  • Subset fonts when practical
  • Consider self-hosting fonts where appropriate
  • Use font-display: swap when appropriate
  • Avoid loading font files that are never used

5. Prevent Layout Shifts

CLS problems often occur when the browser does not know how much space an image, video, advertisement, or dynamically inserted element will require.

Instead of:

<img src="/image.webp" alt="Product">

provide dimensions:

<img
    src="/image.webp"
    width="800"
    height="500"
    alt="Product"
>

You should also reserve space for dynamic content such as ads, embedded media, banners, and asynchronously loaded components.

  • Set image width and height
  • Reserve space for advertisements
  • Reserve space for embedded content
  • Avoid inserting content above existing content unexpectedly
  • Be careful when dynamically changing dimensions

6. Improve Server Response Time and TTFB

Frontend optimization is not enough if the server takes too long to return the initial document.

TTFB — Time to First Byte is useful when investigating how quickly the server begins responding.

When investigating slow server response, check:

  • Server processing time
  • Database queries
  • Slow API calls
  • PHP or Laravel application performance
  • WordPress plugins and database queries
  • Server configuration
  • Page and object caching
  • CDN configuration
  • Hosting resources
  • Redirect chains

A slow backend can delay the browser from discovering and downloading important resources, which can make it harder to achieve a good LCP.

7. Use Effective Caching

Browser and server-side caching can reduce repeated work and prevent visitors from downloading the same static resources unnecessarily.

Static assets such as CSS, JavaScript, images, fonts, and SVG files can generally be cached with appropriate cache headers.

app.css
app.js
hero.webp
logo.svg
font.woff2

Versioned or fingerprinted asset names are useful when using long cache lifetimes:

app.8f32a.css
app.91a7d.js

When the asset changes, the filename can change as well, allowing the browser to safely fetch the new version.

8. Reduce Third-Party Scripts

Analytics, chat widgets, advertising scripts, tracking tools, social embeds, and other third-party resources can add network requests and JavaScript execution to your page.

Review every third-party script and ask whether it is actually needed.

  • Remove unnecessary third-party scripts
  • Load non-critical integrations later
  • Review third-party JavaScript execution time
  • Avoid loading the same library multiple times
  • Check whether widgets are needed on every page

Reducing unnecessary third-party work can help improve loading performance and responsiveness.

9. Optimize for Mobile

A website that performs well on a powerful desktop can behave very differently on a mobile device or slower network.

Always test both mobile and desktop experiences.

  • Test on mobile devices
  • Test slower network conditions
  • Serve appropriately sized images
  • Reduce unnecessary JavaScript
  • Check mobile Core Web Vitals
  • Test real-user data when available

Which Image Technique Should You Use?

Different image formats — Use the Picture element with Source elements to provide modern formats such as AVIF and WebP with suitable fallbacks.

Different crops for mobile and desktop — Use the Picture element with responsive media conditions when mobile and desktop need different image compositions.

Different sizes of the same image — Use responsive image sources with srcset and sizes so the browser can select an appropriate image size.

Images below the fold — Use lazy loading for images that are not immediately visible.

Main LCP / hero image — Avoid lazy loading the primary LCP image. Consider giving it higher loading priority when appropriate.

Prevent layout shifts — Provide explicit image width and height so the browser can reserve the required space before the image loads.

Image accessibility — Use meaningful alternative text that describes the purpose or content of the image.

Image discoverability — Use standard HTML image elements for meaningful images so they can be properly discovered and understood.

My Performance Optimization Checklist

  1. Run PageSpeed Insights on the target page
  2. Check both lab and field data when available
  3. Identify the LCP element
  4. Optimize the LCP resource
  5. Optimize and resize images
  6. Use responsive images with srcset and sizes
  7. Use <picture> when different sources are needed
  8. Lazy-load appropriate below-the-fold images
  9. Reserve dimensions for images and dynamic content
  10. Remove genuinely unused CSS
  11. Keep critical CSS lean
  12. Optimize JavaScript and reduce long tasks
  13. Reduce unnecessary third-party scripts
  14. Optimize fonts and reduce unnecessary font files
  15. Improve server response time and TTFB
  16. Use effective browser and server caching
  17. Test mobile and desktop performance
  18. Monitor real-user Core Web Vitals

Performance Optimization Workflow

PageSpeed Analysis
        ↓
Check Lab + Field Data
        ↓
Identify LCP / INP / CLS Issues
        ↓
Optimize Images
        ↓
Optimize CSS
        ↓
Optimize JavaScript
        ↓
Optimize Fonts
        ↓
Reduce Third-Party Work
        ↓
Improve Server Response / TTFB
        ↓
Enable Effective Caching
        ↓
Prevent Layout Shifts
        ↓
Test Mobile + Desktop
        ↓
Monitor Real User Data
        ↓
Repeat

Tools I Use

Google PageSpeed Insights — Analyze website performance and Core Web Vitals using lab data and, when available, real-user data.

web.dev Performance — Learn performance concepts, optimization techniques, and modern web performance best practices.

web.dev Image Performance — Practical guidance for optimizing image formats, sizing, compression, responsive images, and loading behavior.

Chrome DevTools — Inspect network requests, CSS, JavaScript, rendering, performance, and resource usage.

Lighthouse — Run lab-based audits for performance, accessibility, best practices, and SEO.

Google Search Console — Monitor Core Web Vitals, search performance, and available real-user page experience data.

Final Thoughts

Performance optimization is not about blindly chasing a 100/100 PageSpeed score.

The real goal is to build a website that loads quickly, responds quickly, remains visually stable, and works well for real users across different devices and network conditions.

Start with the biggest bottleneck — whether it is an oversized image, render-blocking CSS, JavaScript execution, fonts, server response time, database queries, or third-party resources.

Measure the problem, make a focused improvement, test again, and monitor the real-world result.

Measure → Optimize → Test → Monitor → Repeat.

posts.title: Deploying Dockerized Laravel Apps on Hostinger VPS with Plesk & Cloudflare
posts.summary: Deploying a Laravel application is more than simply uploading files to a server. A production application needs a reliable environment for PHP, the database, web server, queues, storage, environment variables, and domain routing.
posts.content:
In my deployment workflows, I used a Hostinger VPS with Docker, Docker Compose, Plesk, and Cloudflare to run a containerized Laravel application while keeping domain and server management straightforward.

This approach makes it possible to keep the application environment isolated and reproducible while using Plesk for server and domain management.

Why Dockerize a Laravel Application?

A Laravel application usually depends on multiple services and system requirements such as PHP, PHP extensions, Nginx, MySQL, Redis, queues, scheduled tasks, and other supporting services.

Installing everything directly on a VPS can make deployments difficult to reproduce and maintain.

Docker allows these services to run in isolated containers with clearly defined configurations.

  • Consistent development and production environments
  • Isolated application dependencies
  • Easy service management with Docker Compose
  • Simple application rebuilds and deployments
  • Better separation between application services
  • More predictable server configuration

Deployment Architecture

The basic architecture can be organized like this:

Domain
   |
   v
Cloudflare DNS
   |
   v
Hostinger VPS
   |
   v
Plesk / Web Routing
   |
   v
Docker
   |
   +----------------------+
   |                      |
   v                      v
Nginx                  PHP-FPM
   |                      |
   +----------+-----------+
              |
              v
           Laravel
              |
              v
            MySQL

Each layer has a specific responsibility. Cloudflare handles DNS and optional edge-level services, Plesk provides server and domain management, Docker manages the application services, and Laravel runs inside the application container environment.

1. Prepare the Laravel Application

Before deploying, make sure the Laravel application is production-ready. The application should have the correct environment configuration, dependencies, database migrations, storage configuration, and application key.

Install production dependencies:

composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader

Build frontend assets if the application uses Vite or another frontend build process:

npm install
npm run build

The production environment should never rely on local development configuration.

2. Create the Dockerfile

The Dockerfile defines the environment required to run the Laravel application.

A simplified PHP-FPM Dockerfile can look like this:

FROM php:8.3-fpm

WORKDIR /var/www

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y \
    git \
    unzip \
    libzip-dev \
    libpng-dev \
    libonig-dev \
    libxml2-dev \
    && docker-php-ext-install \
    pdo_mysql \
    mbstring \
    exif \
    pcntl \
    bcmath \
    gd \
    zip

COPY --from=composer:2 /usr/bin/composer /usr/bin/composer

COPY . .

RUN composer install \
    --no-dev \
    --optimize-autoloader

RUN chown -R www-data:www-data \
    storage \
    bootstrap/cache

EXPOSE 9000

CMD ["php-fpm"]

The exact PHP extensions should be adjusted according to the Laravel application's requirements.

3. Configure Docker Compose

Docker Compose can be used to define the application services together. A typical setup can contain Laravel/PHP-FPM, Nginx, and MySQL.

services:

  app:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
    container_name: laravel_app
    restart: unless-stopped
    working_dir: /var/www
    volumes:
      - ./:/var/www
    networks:
      - laravel

  nginx:
    image: nginx:alpine
    container_name: laravel_nginx
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "8080:80"
    volumes:
      - ./:/var/www
      - ./docker/nginx/default.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
    depends_on:
      - app
    networks:
      - laravel

  mysql:
    image: mysql:8.0
    container_name: laravel_mysql
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      MYSQL_DATABASE: laravel
      MYSQL_USER: laravel
      MYSQL_PASSWORD: change-this-password
      MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: change-this-root-password
    volumes:
      - mysql_data:/var/lib/mysql
    networks:
      - laravel

networks:
  laravel:

volumes:
  mysql_data:

In a real production deployment, passwords and other sensitive values should be stored securely rather than committed to source control.

4. Configure Nginx

Nginx handles incoming HTTP requests and forwards PHP requests to the PHP-FPM container.

A basic configuration can look like this:

server {
    listen 80;
    server_name example.com www.example.com;

    root /var/www/public;
    index index.php index.html;

    location / {
        try_files $uri $uri/ /index.php?$query_string;
    }

    location ~ \.php$ {
        try_files $uri =404;

        fastcgi_pass app:9000;
        fastcgi_index index.php;

        include fastcgi_params;

        fastcgi_param SCRIPT_FILENAME
            $document_root$fastcgi_script_name;
    }

    location ~ /\.(?!well-known).* {
        deny all;
    }
}

The important part is that Nginx passes PHP requests to the PHP-FPM service using the Docker service name.

fastcgi_pass app:9000;

5. Configure Laravel Environment Variables

The production environment needs its own configuration.

APP_NAME="Laravel Application"
APP_ENV=production
APP_DEBUG=false
APP_URL=https://example.com

DB_CONNECTION=mysql
DB_HOST=mysql
DB_PORT=3306
DB_DATABASE=laravel
DB_USERNAME=laravel
DB_PASSWORD=your-secure-password

Notice that the database host is the Docker Compose service name:

DB_HOST=mysql

Containers communicate with each other through the Docker network, so Laravel does not need to connect to MySQL using localhost.

6. Start the Docker Containers

Once the Docker configuration is ready, build and start the services:

docker compose up -d --build

Check whether the containers are running:

docker compose ps

If a container is not behaving as expected, inspect its logs:

docker compose logs app
docker compose logs nginx
docker compose logs mysql

Following logs is especially useful when troubleshooting PHP extensions, permissions, database connections, or Nginx configuration issues.

7. Run Laravel Production Commands

After the application containers are running, Laravel's production configuration and caches can be prepared.

docker compose exec app php artisan key:generate

docker compose exec app php artisan migrate --force

docker compose exec app php artisan storage:link

docker compose exec app php artisan config:cache

docker compose exec app php artisan route:cache

docker compose exec app php artisan view:cache

Only run commands such as migrations when you understand their effect on the production database. Database backups should be part of the deployment process.

8. Configure Plesk

Plesk can be used as the management layer for the VPS, domains, DNS-related configuration, SSL, and web hosting settings.

The basic workflow is:

  1. Create or configure the domain in Plesk.
  2. Configure the domain's DNS and routing.
  3. Point the domain toward the VPS.
  4. Configure the application/web server routing.
  5. Enable HTTPS.
  6. Verify that the domain reaches the Dockerized application.

The exact Plesk configuration depends on how Docker and the web server are exposed on the VPS. The important point is to keep the public domain routing separate from the internal Docker service communication.

9. Connect the Domain Through Cloudflare

Cloudflare can be placed in front of the VPS to manage DNS and provide additional edge-level services.

A basic DNS flow looks like:

User
  |
  v
example.com
  |
  v
Cloudflare DNS
  |
  v
Hostinger VPS
  |
  v
Plesk / Web Server
  |
  v
Dockerized Laravel Application

When configuring DNS, make sure the domain points to the correct server and that the VPS firewall allows the required web traffic.

10. SSL and HTTPS

Production Laravel applications should use HTTPS.

After the domain is correctly routed, configure an SSL certificate and verify that the application works through:

https://example.com

Also make sure Laravel's production URL matches the HTTPS domain:

APP_URL=https://example.com

HTTPS is particularly important for applications handling authentication, payments, APIs, and other sensitive requests.

11. File and Storage Permissions

Laravel needs write access to specific directories.

storage/
bootstrap/cache/

For example:

docker compose exec app chown -R www-data:www-data storage bootstrap/cache

docker compose exec app chmod -R 775 storage bootstrap/cache

Avoid giving the entire application directory unnecessary write permissions. Permissions should be limited to the directories that actually require them.

12. Laravel Queue Workers

Applications that use queues for emails, notifications, background jobs, or other asynchronous operations need a worker process running in production.

A basic worker command is:

php artisan queue:work --tries=3 --timeout=90

For a Dockerized application, the worker can also be defined as a separate service in Docker Compose.

queue:
  build:
    context: .
    dockerfile: Dockerfile
  restart: unless-stopped
  working_dir: /var/www
  command: php artisan queue:work --tries=3 --timeout=90
  volumes:
    - ./:/var/www
  depends_on:
    - app
  networks:
    - laravel

Separating workers from the web process makes it easier to scale and monitor background workloads independently.

13. Laravel Scheduled Tasks

Laravel applications may also require scheduled tasks for reminders, cleanup jobs, reports, notifications, or recurring business processes.

The scheduler can be executed using:

php artisan schedule:run

A production server can invoke this command periodically through a scheduler such as cron.

* * * * * cd /var/www && php artisan schedule:run >> /dev/null 2>&1

14. Production Deployment Workflow

Once the initial infrastructure is configured, deployments can follow a predictable process.

Pull latest code
      ↓
Install/update dependencies
      ↓
Build frontend assets
      ↓
Build Docker images
      ↓
Start updated containers
      ↓
Run database migrations
      ↓
Clear and rebuild Laravel caches
      ↓
Restart queue workers
      ↓
Check application logs
      ↓
Test website and APIs

This makes deployments more repeatable and reduces the risk of manually changing production servers.

15. Useful Docker Commands

These are some of the commands I commonly use when managing a Dockerized Laravel application.

# Check running containers
docker compose ps

# Start containers
docker compose up -d

# Rebuild containers
docker compose up -d --build

# Stop containers
docker compose down

# View application logs
docker compose logs -f app

# View Nginx logs
docker compose logs -f nginx

# Enter Laravel container
docker compose exec app bash

# Run Laravel migrations
docker compose exec app php artisan migrate --force

# Clear Laravel caches
docker compose exec app php artisan optimize:clear

# Rebuild Laravel caches
docker compose exec app php artisan optimize

# Restart services
docker compose restart

Common Deployment Challenges

Docker and Port Conflicts

Running multiple applications on the same VPS can create port conflicts. Each application's public entry point needs a clear routing strategy.

Domain Routing

Connecting a domain managed through Plesk to an application running inside Docker requires careful routing between the public web server and the internal container network.

Cloudflare DNS

DNS records, proxy settings, SSL modes, and origin configuration need to be consistent with the actual VPS and web-server setup.

Container Permissions

Laravel storage and cache directories can produce errors when the container user does not have the required permissions.

Environment Variables

Production applications often fail because environment values are missing or still point to local development services.

Database Connectivity

Docker containers should communicate through their Docker network using service names rather than assuming localhost refers to another container.

Application Updates

Updating the application requires more than replacing source files. Dependencies, frontend assets, database migrations, caches, and workers may all need to be updated.

Production Deployment Checklist

  • Production environment variables configured
  • APP_DEBUG disabled
  • Secure database credentials configured
  • Docker images built successfully
  • All required containers running
  • Database migrations completed safely
  • Laravel caches optimized
  • Storage permissions verified
  • Queue workers running where required
  • Scheduled tasks configured where required
  • Domain correctly routed through Plesk
  • Cloudflare DNS correctly configured
  • HTTPS/SSL verified
  • Application logs checked
  • Production website and APIs tested
  • Database and application backups configured

Final Thoughts

Dockerizing a Laravel application and deploying it on a VPS provides a practical way to create a more consistent and maintainable production environment.

Using Docker Compose for application services, Plesk for server and domain management, and Cloudflare for DNS and edge-level configuration creates a workflow where each part of the infrastructure has a clear responsibility.

The most important lesson is that deployment should be treated as an engineering workflow rather than simply uploading a Laravel project to a server.

Build → Configure → Deploy → Route → Secure → Monitor → Repeat.

posts.title: Syncing Bokun Bookings with Google Contacts
posts.summary: How to turn every Bokun booking into a Google contact with Laravel: receive the webhook, save to MySQL first, then create or update the contact through the People API without ever creating a duplicate.
posts.content:
A tour business takes bookings in Bokun, but the team answers customers from their phones. If every booking also becomes a Google contact, a call or WhatsApp message from a customer shows their name instead of an unknown number. The hard part is not creating contacts. It is making sure the same customer never ends up in the address book three times.

This article walks through the flow in Laravel: receive the booking, save it in MySQL, then create or update the Google contact from a queued job.

1. Receive the booking

Bokun can call a webhook URL when a booking is created, changed or cancelled. Keep the endpoint small: accept the request, queue a job, and answer straight away.

// routes/api.php
Route::post('/webhooks/bokun', BokunWebhookController::class);
class BokunWebhookController extends Controller
{
    public function __invoke(Request $request)
    {
        $bookingId = $request->input('bookingId');

        abort_if(blank($bookingId), 422);

        SyncBokunBooking::dispatch((string) $bookingId);

        return response()->noContent(200);
    }
}

Treat the webhook as a notification, not as data you trust. Take only the booking ID from it, then fetch the booking from Bokun's API yourself. A forged request can then do no more than trigger a harmless re-sync of a booking that really exists.

Bokun's REST API signs each request with your access key and secret key. You send the date, the access key and an HMAC-SHA1 signature in the X-Bokun-Date, X-Bokun-AccessKey and X-Bokun-Signature headers. The exact string to sign is described in the Bokun developer documentation, so follow that rather than copying a snippet from a blog.

2. Save to MySQL first

Your own database is the source of truth, not Google. Save the booking and the customer before you talk to any other API, so a Google outage never loses a booking.

Schema::create('customers', function (Blueprint $table) {
    $table->id();
    $table->string('email')->unique();
    $table->string('phone')->nullable();
    $table->string('name');
    $table->string('google_resource_name')->nullable();
    $table->timestamp('google_synced_at')->nullable();
    $table->timestamps();
});

Two details matter here. Normalise the email (trim it and lowercase it) before saving, so Asha@Example.com and asha@example.com are one customer. And put a unique index on it, so the database enforces that rule even when two webhooks arrive at the same moment.

$customer = Customer::updateOrCreate(
    ['email' => Str::lower(trim($booking['customer']['email']))],
    [
        'name' => trim($booking['customer']['firstName'].' '.$booking['customer']['lastName']),
        'phone' => $booking['customer']['phoneNumber'] ?? null,
    ],
);

3. Connect to Google

Contacts belong to a Google account, so the People API needs OAuth consent from that account, with the scope https://www.googleapis.com/auth/contacts. Ask for offline access so you receive a refresh token, and store that token encrypted. Laravel's encrypted cast is enough:

protected function casts(): array
{
    return ['google_refresh_token' => 'encrypted'];
}

Enable the People API for your project in the Google Cloud Console before testing, otherwise every call fails with a permission error that looks like a code bug.

4. Avoid duplicates

Google does not stop you from creating the same contact twice. You have to check first, and one check is not enough. Use three layers.

Remember what you created

When Google creates a contact it returns a resourceName such as people/c123456789. Save it on the customer row. The next time that customer books, you update that exact contact and never search at all. This one column removes most duplicates.

Search before creating

If there is no saved resourceName, the contact may still exist because someone added it by hand. Search by email:

GET https://people.googleapis.com/v1/people:searchContacts
    ?query=asha@example.com
    &readMask=names,emailAddresses,phoneNumbers

Two things about search catch people out. Google asks you to send one warm-up request with an empty query before the first real search, and a contact created seconds ago may not appear in results yet. That delay is exactly why the saved resourceName comes first.

One job per customer at a time

A booking that is created and then immediately edited sends two webhooks. If both jobs run together, both search, both find nothing, and both create. Make the job unique per customer:

class SyncCustomerToGoogle implements ShouldQueue, ShouldBeUnique
{
    public int $tries = 5;

    public function __construct(public Customer $customer) {}

    public function uniqueId(): string
    {
        return (string) $this->customer->id;
    }

    public function backoff(): array
    {
        return [30, 120, 300, 900];
    }
}

5. Create or update

Creating is a single request. Save the resourceName from the response immediately.

$person = Http::withToken($accessToken)
    ->post('https://people.googleapis.com/v1/people:createContact', [
        'names' => [['givenName' => $customer->name]],
        'emailAddresses' => [['value' => $customer->email]],
        'phoneNumbers' => $customer->phone ? [['value' => $customer->phone]] : [],
    ])
    ->throw()
    ->json();

$customer->update([
    'google_resource_name' => $person['resourceName'],
    'google_synced_at' => now(),
]);

Updating has one rule that causes most failed requests: you must send the contact's current etag, and you must list which fields you are changing in updatePersonFields. Fetch the contact, then update it:

$current = Http::withToken($accessToken)
    ->get("https://people.googleapis.com/v1/{$customer->google_resource_name}", [
        'personFields' => 'names,emailAddresses,phoneNumbers',
    ])
    ->throw()
    ->json();

Http::withToken($accessToken)
    ->patch("https://people.googleapis.com/v1/{$customer->google_resource_name}:updateContact?updatePersonFields=names,phoneNumbers", [
        'etag' => $current['etag'],
        'names' => [['givenName' => $customer->name]],
        'phoneNumbers' => $customer->phone ? [['value' => $customer->phone]] : [],
    ])
    ->throw();

If someone edits the contact on their phone between your two requests, the etag no longer matches and Google rejects the update. Let the job fail and retry: the next attempt fetches the new etag. If the fetch returns a 404, the contact was deleted by hand. Clear the saved resourceName and create it again.

6. Errors worth handling

ResponseWhat it usually meansWhat to do
401The access token expired.Use the refresh token to get a new one and retry once.
403The People API is not enabled, or the scope is missing.Enable the API and reconnect the Google account with the contacts scope.
400 on updateThe etag is out of date or updatePersonFields is missing.Fetch the contact again and retry.
404The contact was deleted in Google.Clear the saved resourceName and create a new contact.
429You are sending requests too quickly.Let the queue retry with a delay. Do not sync a whole backlog in one burst.

Checklist

  • The webhook only queues a job and returns 200.
  • The booking is fetched from Bokun with a signed request, not trusted from the webhook body.
  • MySQL is written first, with a unique index on the normalised email.
  • The Google resourceName is saved and used for every later update.
  • Search runs only when no resourceName is saved.
  • The sync job is unique per customer and retries with a delay.
  • Updates send the current etag and updatePersonFields.
  • The refresh token is stored encrypted.

The reference for every People API call used here is in Google's People API documentation.

posts.title: Setting Up Cloudflared Tunnels for Zero-Configuration Local-to-Live Staging
posts.summary: Give a local project a public HTTPS address with one cloudflared command: quick tunnels for demos, named tunnels for webhook testing, the Laravel settings that make it work, and how to keep it safe.
posts.content:
A client wants to see the feature today, but it only exists on your laptop. Or a payment provider needs a public HTTPS address for its webhook, and you are still developing locally. A Cloudflare Tunnel solves both: one command gives your local server a public HTTPS URL, with no deployment, no router setup and no open ports.

How it works

You run a small program called cloudflared next to your app. It opens an outbound connection to Cloudflare. Cloudflare gives you a public hostname and forwards every request for that hostname back down the connection to your local port. Because the connection starts from your machine, nothing has to be opened on your router or firewall.

Install cloudflared

# macOS
brew install cloudflared

# Windows
winget install --id Cloudflare.cloudflared

# Check it
cloudflared --version

Linux packages are listed on Cloudflare's downloads page.

Quick tunnel: a public URL in one command

Start your app as usual, then point cloudflared at its port. You do not need a Cloudflare account for this.

php artisan serve --port=8000

# in a second terminal
cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:8000

The output contains an address ending in trycloudflare.com. Send that link to your client, or paste it into a webhook settings page. It works for as long as the command keeps running.

Quick tunnels are for short tests. The address is random and changes every time you restart, so anything you configured with the old address stops working. For anything you will use for more than an afternoon, create a named tunnel.

Named tunnel: your own stable address

A named tunnel uses a hostname on a domain you manage in Cloudflare, for example staging.example.com, and keeps it between restarts.

# 1. Sign in (opens the browser once)
cloudflared tunnel login

# 2. Create the tunnel
cloudflared tunnel create staging

# 3. Point a hostname at it
cloudflared tunnel route dns staging staging.example.com

Then describe where requests should go in ~/.cloudflared/config.yml:

tunnel: staging
credentials-file: /Users/you/.cloudflared/<TUNNEL_ID>.json

ingress:
  - hostname: staging.example.com
    service: http://localhost:8000
  - service: http_status:404

The last rule is required. It tells the tunnel what to answer for any hostname that does not match. Start it with:

cloudflared tunnel run staging

You can add more hostnames to the same file, for example one for the Laravel app and one for a separate front end, each pointing at a different local port.

Laravel settings that matter

The tunnel serves HTTPS to the visitor but talks plain HTTP to your local app. Without a little setup, Laravel builds http:// links, and the browser blocks them as mixed content. Three changes fix it.

Trust the proxy

// bootstrap/app.php
->withMiddleware(function (Middleware $middleware) {
    $middleware->trustProxies(at: '*');
})

This lets Laravel read the forwarded headers and understand that the original request was HTTPS. Only trust all proxies in a local or staging environment.

Set the public address

APP_URL=https://staging.example.com

Run php artisan config:clear afterwards. Generated links, emails, signed URLs and file URLs all use this value.

Serve built assets

The Vite development server runs on its own port, which the tunnel does not expose, so a visitor would see a page with no styles. The simple fix is to build the assets and stop the development server while you share the link:

npm run build

Testing webhooks

This is where tunnels save the most time. Stripe, Razorpay, WhatsApp, Bokun and Shopify all need a public HTTPS address to send events to. Use the tunnel address as the webhook URL and you can set breakpoints and read logs on your own machine while real events arrive.

  • Use a named tunnel, so the address in the provider's dashboard does not need changing every morning.
  • Keep signature verification switched on. A tunnel is public, and anyone who learns the address can post to it.
  • Remember that webhook routes must not require a CSRF token.

Keep it safe

  • The address is public. Anyone who has it can open your local app. Share it only with the people who need it.
  • Turn off debug pages. With APP_DEBUG=true, an error page can show environment values to a stranger.
  • Do not use real customer data in a database you expose this way.
  • Add a login in front for anything that stays up. Cloudflare Access can require an email code before a visitor reaches your app.
  • Stop the tunnel when the review is over. Press Ctrl+C and the address stops working.

Common problems

What you seeLikely causeFix
Error 502 on the public addressNothing is listening on the local port.Start your app, and check the port in the command or config.yml matches.
Page loads without stylesAssets point at the Vite development server.Run npm run build and stop npm run dev.
Mixed content warnings, or redirects to http://Laravel does not know the request was HTTPS.Trust the proxy and set APP_URL to the HTTPS address.
Login works, then you are logged outThe session cookie was set for a different domain.Clear SESSION_DOMAIN or set it to the tunnel hostname, then clear the config cache.
The address worked yesterdayIt was a quick tunnel, and the address changed on restart.Switch to a named tunnel.

Which one to use

  • Quick tunnel for a five-minute demo or a one-off test.
  • Named tunnel for webhook development and client review over several days.
  • A real staging server once more than one person needs the app available when your laptop is closed.

Cloudflare's full reference is in the Cloudflare Tunnel documentation.

posts.title: Building Shopify Art Generators with React and Node
posts.summary: How to structure an AI artwork feature for a Shopify store: a React interface, a Node server that keeps every key private, request verification, queued generation and stored results.
posts.content:
A store wants customers to type an idea and get a piece of artwork they can buy as a print. The feature sounds like one API call. In practice the work is everything around that call: keeping the API key out of the browser, proving that a request really came from the store, coping with a response that takes half a minute, and keeping the result so the customer can order it.

This article describes the structure that handles all of that: a React interface, a Node server that owns every secret, and a job that does the slow work.

The one rule: keys stay on the server

Anything shipped to the browser can be read by the visitor, including any key placed in React code or in a VITE_ or NEXT_PUBLIC_ variable. Someone who copies an image API key can generate images at your cost until you notice the bill.

So the browser never talks to the image service. React sends the prompt to your own Node server. The server checks the request, adds the key, and calls the image service itself.

Prove the request came from the store

Your generate endpoint is on the public internet. Without a check, anyone can call it directly. Which check you use depends on where the React interface runs.

Inside the Shopify admin: session tokens

An embedded app gets a short-lived session token from Shopify App Bridge and sends it in the Authorization header. It is a JWT signed with your app's secret. On the server, verify the signature and expiry, and read the shop from it. Shopify's Node library does this for you:

import { shopifyApp } from '@shopify/shopify-app-express';

const shopify = shopifyApp({ /* api keys, scopes, session storage */ });

app.use('/api/*', shopify.validateAuthenticatedSession());

app.post('/api/generate', async (req, res) => {
    const { shop } = res.locals.shopify.session;
    // the request is from a signed-in user of this shop
});

On the storefront: the app proxy signature

Customers on the storefront have no admin session. Use an app proxy instead. The storefront calls a path on the shop's own domain, such as /apps/art/generate, and Shopify forwards it to your server with a signature parameter. Recalculate that signature with your app secret and compare:

import crypto from 'node:crypto';

function isFromShopify(query, secret) {
    const { signature, ...params } = query;

    const message = Object.keys(params)
        .sort()
        .map((key) => `${key}=${[].concat(params[key]).join(',')}`)
        .join('');

    const expected = crypto.createHmac('sha256', secret).update(message).digest('hex');

    return signature?.length === expected.length
        && crypto.timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(signature), Buffer.from(expected));
}

The forwarded request also carries the shop domain and, when the customer is logged in, their customer ID. Use those for limits and for saving results. Do not accept a shop name or customer ID from the request body.

Validate and limit before spending money

Every accepted request costs you something, so reject bad ones early:

  • Trim the prompt and enforce a maximum length.
  • Refuse empty prompts and prompts that are only whitespace.
  • Limit requests per customer and per shop, for example a few per minute and a daily cap.
  • Allow only the sizes and styles you actually sell. Do not pass arbitrary options from the browser to the image service.

Generation is slow, so make it a job

Creating an image can take anywhere from a few seconds to over a minute. Holding one HTTP request open that long fails often: proxies time out, phones switch networks, customers reload. Split the work in two.

  1. POST /generate validates the request, saves a row with the status pending, queues a job and returns the job ID immediately.
  2. GET /generate/:id returns the current status, and the image URL once it is done.
app.post('/apps/art/generate', async (req, res) => {
    if (!isFromShopify(req.query, process.env.SHOPIFY_API_SECRET)) {
        return res.status(401).json({ error: 'Invalid signature' });
    }

    const prompt = String(req.body.prompt ?? '').trim();

    if (prompt.length < 3 || prompt.length > 400) {
        return res.status(422).json({ error: 'Describe your artwork in 3 to 400 characters.' });
    }

    const job = await db.generations.create({
        shop: req.query.shop,
        customerId: req.query.logged_in_customer_id || null,
        prompt,
        status: 'pending',
    });

    await queue.add('generate-art', { id: job.id });

    res.status(202).json({ id: job.id });
});

The worker is the only place that touches the image service:

import OpenAI from 'openai';

const openai = new OpenAI({ apiKey: process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY });

async function generateArt({ id }) {
    const job = await db.generations.find(id);

    try {
        const result = await openai.images.generate({
            model: process.env.IMAGE_MODEL,
            prompt: job.prompt,
            size: '1024x1024',
        });

        const image = Buffer.from(result.data[0].b64_json, 'base64');
        const url = await storage.upload(`art/${job.shop}/${id}.png`, image);

        await db.generations.update(id, { status: 'done', imageUrl: url });
    } catch (error) {
        await db.generations.update(id, { status: 'failed', error: error.message });
    }
}

Keep the model name in an environment variable. Image models are replaced often, and the current names are listed in the image generation guide.

Store the result

The image service returns the picture as data, not as a permanent link. Save the file yourself, in object storage or in the shop's own Shopify Files, and keep a database row with the shop, customer, prompt, image URL and status. That row is what lets a customer come back to their artwork, lets the merchant see what was generated, and lets you attach the image to an order as a line item property.

The React side

The interface has four states: idle, generating, done and failed. Model them explicitly instead of juggling several booleans.

function ArtGenerator() {
    const [state, setState] = useState({ status: 'idle' });

    async function generate(prompt) {
        setState({ status: 'generating' });

        const response = await fetch('/apps/art/generate', {
            method: 'POST',
            headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
            body: JSON.stringify({ prompt }),
        });

        if (!response.ok) {
            const { error } = await response.json();
            return setState({ status: 'failed', error });
        }

        const { id } = await response.json();
        poll(id);
    }

    async function poll(id) {
        const job = await (await fetch(`/apps/art/generate/${id}`)).json();

        if (job.status === 'done') return setState({ status: 'done', imageUrl: job.imageUrl });
        if (job.status === 'failed') return setState({ status: 'failed', error: 'Generation failed. Please try again.' });

        setTimeout(() => poll(id), 2500);
    }

    // render the form, a progress message, the image, or the error
}

Disable the button while a request is running, show a message that explains the wait, and always give the customer a way to try again. Never show the raw error from the image service; log it on the server and show a plain sentence instead.

Checklist

  • No API key appears anywhere in the front-end code or its environment variables.
  • Every request is verified with a session token or the app proxy signature.
  • The shop and customer come from Shopify's signed data, never from the request body.
  • Prompts are validated, and requests are limited per customer and per shop.
  • Generation runs in a queue, and the browser polls for the result.
  • Images are saved to your own storage with a database record.
  • Errors are logged on the server and shown to customers in plain language.
